questiontext.text: What is Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD)?

answer.text: A collaborative practice in which business, development, and testing describe desired behaviour through concrete examples that become executable specifications and living documentation

feedback.text: Correct — BDD centres on shared, example-based descriptions of behaviour that can be run.

answer.text: A tool that automatically generates production code from a UML class diagram

feedback.text: BDD is a collaboration and specification practice, not a code generator from diagrams.

answer.text: A profiling technique for measuring how fast each function runs

feedback.text: That is performance profiling; BDD is about specifying behaviour by example.

answer.text: A branch-coverage metric for deciding when testing is finished

feedback.text: Coverage is a separate idea; BDD describes behaviour collaboratively via examples.

generalfeedback.text: BDD grew out of TDD and emphasises conversation between business, developers, and testers ("the three amigos"). The team agrees on concrete examples of behaviour, writes them in a shared language, and turns them into automated, executable specifications that also serve as living documentation.

questiontext.text: What is Gherkin?

answer.text: A structured, mostly-plain-language syntax (Feature, Scenario, Given/When/Then) for writing BDD specifications that both people and tools can read

feedback.text: Correct — Gherkin is the business-readable, keyword-based language used to write BDD scenarios.

answer.text: A general-purpose programming language that compiles to machine code

feedback.text: Gherkin is a specification syntax, not a compiled programming language.

answer.text: A database query language for retrieving test results

feedback.text: Gherkin describes behaviour scenarios; it is not a query language.

answer.text: A continuous-integration server that runs builds

feedback.text: That is a CI tool; Gherkin is the language scenarios are written in.

generalfeedback.text: Gherkin is the line-oriented language used by Cucumber-style tools. It uses a small set of keywords — Feature, Scenario, Given, When, Then, And, But, Background, Scenario Outline, Examples — so that a specification reads almost like ordinary prose yet can be automated through step definitions.

questiontext.text: In Gherkin, what does the Feature keyword introduce?

answer.text: A named piece of functionality, with a free-text description, that groups together the scenarios illustrating it

feedback.text: Correct — a Feature names a capability and holds the scenarios that describe it.

answer.text: A single test step that checks one expected value

feedback.text: A single step is a Given/When/Then line; a Feature groups whole scenarios.

answer.text: The block of glue code that maps steps to functions

feedback.text: That is a step definition; a Feature is the top-level grouping in a .feature file.

answer.text: A table of example data for a data-driven run

feedback.text: That is an Examples table; a Feature is the named functionality it belongs to.

generalfeedback.text: A .feature file usually begins with one Feature: line naming the capability, optionally followed by a free-text description of its business value. Underneath it come the Scenarios (and optionally a Background and Scenario Outlines) that give concrete examples of that feature's behaviour.

questiontext.text: In Gherkin, what is a Scenario?

answer.text: A single concrete example of the feature's behaviour, expressed as a sequence of Given/When/Then steps

feedback.text: Correct — a Scenario is one concrete illustration of behaviour built from steps.

answer.text: The name of the file that contains the feature

feedback.text: The file is the .feature file; a Scenario is one example inside it.

answer.text: A programming loop that repeats a test many times

feedback.text: A Scenario is a described example, not a loop construct.

answer.text: The random seed used to reproduce a failing run

feedback.text: Gherkin scenarios are concrete examples; there is no random seed involved.

generalfeedback.text: A Scenario captures one concrete case of how the feature should behave: a context (Given), an event (When), and an expected outcome (Then). A feature typically contains several scenarios, each illustrating a different situation.

questiontext.text: What does the Given keyword express in a Gherkin scenario?

answer.text: The context or precondition — the state of the world that must already hold before the behaviour is exercised

feedback.text: Correct — Given establishes the starting context/preconditions.

answer.text: The single action or event that triggers the behaviour

feedback.text: That is the role of When; Given sets up the context beforehand.

answer.text: The expected, observable outcome to be verified

feedback.text: That is the role of Then; Given describes the precondition.

answer.text: The name of the feature under test

feedback.text: The feature name follows Feature:; Given describes the scenario's starting state.

generalfeedback.text: Given puts the system into a known state — a precondition or context — such as "Given the user is logged in". It is setup, not the action being tested, and it should not contain the outcome you intend to check.

questiontext.text: What does the When keyword express in a Gherkin scenario?

answer.text: The action or event under test — ideally a single thing the actor does that triggers the behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — When names the event/action being exercised, ideally just one.

answer.text: The precondition that must already hold beforehand

feedback.text: That is the role of Given; When is the triggering action.

answer.text: The expected result that should be observed afterwards

feedback.text: That is the role of Then; When is the action that leads to it.

answer.text: A comment describing why the scenario exists

feedback.text: When is a behavioural step, not a comment; it names the action.

generalfeedback.text: When describes the event or action that exercises the behaviour, such as "When the user submits the form". A well-written scenario has essentially one When: the single action whose consequences the Then step then verifies.

questiontext.text: What does the Then keyword express in a Gherkin scenario?

answer.text: The expected, observable outcome that should hold after the action — the thing the scenario verifies

feedback.text: Correct — Then states the observable outcome to be checked.

answer.text: The context that must be set up before anything happens

feedback.text: That is the role of Given; Then is the outcome checked at the end.

answer.text: The action the user performs to trigger behaviour

feedback.text: That is the role of When; Then verifies the result of that action.

answer.text: A list of example rows for a data-driven scenario

feedback.text: That is an Examples table; Then states the expected outcome.

generalfeedback.text: Then asserts an observable outcome, e.g. "Then the account balance is 100". It should describe what can be observed (a result, a message, a state), not another action the actor takes — actions belong in When.

questiontext.text:
In Gherkin, what do the And and But keywords do?

Given the user is logged in
And the cart contains 2 items

answer.text: They continue the previous step and take on its type, so a step after Given (via And/But) is still a Given (a precondition here)

feedback.text: Correct — And/But inherit the category of the step they follow.

answer.text: They always introduce a new action, regardless of what came before

feedback.text: No — And/But do not have a fixed type; they inherit the previous step's type.

answer.text: They are comments that the tool ignores

feedback.text: And/But are real steps; they simply share the prior keyword's category.

answer.text: But means the step is expected to fail

feedback.text: But is just a readability continuation; it does not mark an expected failure.

generalfeedback.text: And and But exist purely for readability. A step written with And or But belongs to the same phase (Given, When, or Then) as the most recent such keyword above it. In the example, "And the cart contains 2 items" is another Given (precondition).

questiontext.text: What is a step definition in a BDD tool?

answer.text: Code (glue) that matches a Gherkin step's text and performs the corresponding automation against the system

feedback.text: Correct — a step definition binds a plain-language step to executable code.

answer.text: The plain-language line inside a scenario itself

feedback.text: That is the step; the step definition is the code the step maps to.

answer.text: The Examples table that supplies data to a Scenario Outline

feedback.text: That is an Examples table; a step definition is the glue code behind steps.

answer.text: A comment describing the feature's business value

feedback.text: Step definitions are executable glue code, not comments.

generalfeedback.text: Gherkin steps are plain text; a step definition is the glue code (in Java, Python, C#, JavaScript, etc.) whose pattern matches a step and drives the application. Running a scenario means matching each step to its definition and executing it.

name.text: What Scenario Outline and Examples are

questiontext.text:
What do a Scenario Outline and its Examples table provide?

Scenario Outline: adding items
  When I add <qty> items
  Then the cart shows <qty> items

  Examples:
    | qty |
    | 1   |
    | 5   |

answer.text: A data-driven template with <placeholders> that is run once per data row of the Examples table

feedback.text: Correct — a Scenario Outline is a parameterised template filled in by each Examples row.

answer.text: A way to mark a scenario as skipped during a run

feedback.text: Skipping is done with tags/filters; a Scenario Outline is a data-driven template.

answer.text: The glue code that maps steps to functions

feedback.text: That is a step definition; a Scenario Outline is a parameterised scenario.

answer.text: A shared Given that runs before every scenario

feedback.text: That is Background; a Scenario Outline is a template driven by Examples data.

generalfeedback.text: A Scenario Outline uses <placeholders> in its steps and pairs them with an Examples table. Each data row substitutes its values into the placeholders and runs the scenario once, giving concise data-driven coverage of many similar cases.

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of the Background keyword in a feature file?

answer.text: To hold steps (usually shared Given preconditions) that run before every scenario in the feature, avoiding repetition

feedback.text: Correct — Background factors out the common setup steps for all scenarios in the feature.

answer.text: To define the expected outcome shared by all scenarios

feedback.text: Outcomes are Then steps per scenario; Background holds shared setup, typically Givens.

answer.text: To supply the data rows for a Scenario Outline

feedback.text: That is an Examples table; Background is shared setup run before each scenario.

answer.text: To store the glue code for the feature's steps

feedback.text: Glue code lives in step definitions; Background is common Gherkin setup.

generalfeedback.text: Background lets you write setup steps once and have them execute before each scenario in the feature. It normally contains Given steps that establish common context (e.g. "Given the user is logged in"), keeping individual scenarios focused and free of repeated setup.

questiontext.text: What are Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave, and JBehave?

answer.text: BDD tools that parse Gherkin-style scenarios and run them by matching steps to step definitions

feedback.text: Correct — these are BDD frameworks that execute Gherkin scenarios via step definitions.

answer.text: Code-coverage measurement tools

feedback.text: They are BDD execution tools, not coverage measurers.

answer.text: Version-control systems

feedback.text: They run BDD scenarios; they are not version-control systems.

answer.text: Static type checkers

feedback.text: They execute behaviour specifications; they are not type checkers.

generalfeedback.text: Cucumber (Ruby/Java/JS), SpecFlow (.NET), Behave (Python), and JBehave (Java) are BDD frameworks. They read Gherkin (or Gherkin-like) scenarios, match each step to its step definition, and execute the automation, reporting each scenario as pass or fail.

questiontext.text:
Which Gherkin keyword best fits this line, given that it states a starting condition rather than an action or a result?

___ the user has an account with a balance of 100

answer.text: Given — it is a precondition/context

feedback.text: Correct — an existing state that holds before the action is a Given.

answer.text: When — it is the triggering action

feedback.text: No action is performed here; this is setup, which is a Given.

answer.text: Then — it is the expected outcome

feedback.text: Nothing is being verified yet; a starting balance is a precondition (Given).

answer.text: Feature — it names the functionality

feedback.text: Feature names the capability; this line describes a precondition, so it is a Given.

generalfeedback.text: "The user has an account with a balance of 100" describes the state of the world before anything happens — a precondition. Preconditions are expressed with Given.

questiontext.text:
Which Gherkin keyword best fits this line, which describes the actor performing the event under test?

___ the user withdraws 30 from the account

answer.text: When — it is the action/event under test

feedback.text: Correct — the actor performing the triggering event is a When step.

answer.text: Given — it is a precondition

feedback.text: This is the action being exercised, not setup; that is a When.

answer.text: Then — it is the expected outcome

feedback.text: Withdrawing is the action, not the outcome to verify; that is a When.

answer.text: Background — it is shared setup

feedback.text: Background holds shared Givens; an action performed by the actor is a When.

generalfeedback.text: "The user withdraws 30" is the event that triggers the behaviour being tested, so it is a When step. The resulting balance would then be checked in a Then step.

questiontext.text: In Gherkin, the Then keyword is used to state the expected, observable outcome that the scenario verifies.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — Then states the observable outcome being checked.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Then does express the expected outcome; the precondition is Given and the action is When.

generalfeedback.text: The Given/When/Then structure maps to precondition / action / expected outcome. Then is the assertion step: it describes what should be observable after the When action, which is exactly the outcome the scenario verifies.

questiontext.text:
Which keyword correctly completes the last line, which states the result to be verified?

Given the cart contains 2 items
When the user removes 1 item
___ the cart contains 1 item

answer.text: Then

feedback.text: Correct — the final line asserts the observable result, so it is a Then step.

answer.text: Given

feedback.text: Given is the precondition at the top; the result line after the action is a Then.

answer.text: When

feedback.text: The action (removing an item) is already the When; the result is a Then.

answer.text: Background

feedback.text: Background is feature-level shared setup, not the outcome line of a scenario.

generalfeedback.text: The scenario sets context (Given), performs one action (When), and then checks the observable result. "The cart contains 1 item" is that verified outcome, so it takes Then.

questiontext.text:
How many times does this Scenario Outline run?

Scenario Outline: login attempts
  When I sign in as <user>
  Then I see <result>

  Examples:
    | user  | result   |
    | alice | welcome  |
    | bob   | welcome  |
    | mallory | blocked |

answer.text: 3 — once per data row in the Examples table

feedback.text: Correct — the header row is not counted; the 3 data rows produce 3 runs.

answer.text: 4 — the header row counts as a run too

feedback.text: The header row only names the columns; it is not a run. Only the 3 data rows count.

answer.text: 1 — a Scenario Outline always runs once

feedback.text: A Scenario Outline runs once per data row, so with 3 rows it runs 3 times.

answer.text: 6 — rows times columns

feedback.text: Runs equal the number of data rows (3), not rows multiplied by columns.

generalfeedback.text: A Scenario Outline expands to one concrete scenario per data row of its Examples table. Here there are 3 data rows (the first line is the column header), so it runs 3 times.

questiontext.text: You notice the same two Given steps at the top of every scenario in a feature. What is the idiomatic fix?

answer.text: Move those shared Given steps into a Background block so they run before each scenario without repetition

feedback.text: Correct — Background is exactly for common setup shared by all scenarios in the feature.

answer.text: Move them into an Examples table

feedback.text: Examples supply data to a Scenario Outline, not shared setup for ordinary scenarios.

answer.text: Delete them from every scenario and rely on the tool to infer the context

feedback.text: The tool infers nothing; the shared setup must be stated once in a Background.

answer.text: Convert each scenario into a step definition

feedback.text: Step definitions are glue code; the repetition of Gherkin setup is solved by Background.

generalfeedback.text: Background collects steps — usually common Given preconditions — that should run before every scenario in the feature. It removes duplicated setup and keeps each scenario focused on what makes it distinct.

questiontext.text:
Two scenarios test the same login behaviour. Which is the better-written (declarative, business-readable) one?

A

Given I am a registered user
When I log in with valid credentials
Then I see my dashboard

B

Given I open "/login"
When I type "alice" into field #user
And I type "secret" into field #pass
And I click the button with id "submit"
Then the element #dash is visible

answer.text: A — it states the behaviour at a business level, independent of UI details

feedback.text: Correct — declarative scenarios describe intent and survive UI changes.

answer.text: B — it is better because it lists every UI click and field id

feedback.text: B is imperative: it is brittle, hard to read, and breaks when the UI changes.

answer.text: Both are equally good; style does not matter

feedback.text: Style matters: the declarative version is more readable and more maintainable.

answer.text: Neither is valid Gherkin

feedback.text: Both are valid Gherkin; A is simply the better-written, declarative form.

generalfeedback.text: Declarative scenarios (A) describe what the user is trying to achieve in business terms, hiding UI mechanics inside step definitions. Imperative scenarios (B) hard-code clicks, field ids, and selectors, making them brittle and hard to read. Prefer declarative.

name.text: Given is setup, not the action

questiontext.text: Which line is an appropriate Given step (setup/precondition) rather than an action?

answer.text: Given the user already has 3 unread messages

feedback.text: Correct — this establishes a starting state, which is what Given is for.

answer.text: Given the user clicks the "Mark all read" button

feedback.text: Clicking is an action; it belongs in a When, not a Given.

answer.text: Given the inbox shows 0 unread messages afterwards

feedback.text: That is an expected outcome; it belongs in a Then, not a Given.

answer.text: Given the user submits the registration form

feedback.text: Submitting is an action; it belongs in a When, not a Given.

generalfeedback.text: A Given establishes context: a state that already holds before the behaviour is exercised. "The user already has 3 unread messages" is such a state. Clicks and submissions are actions (When); results checked afterwards are outcomes (Then).

name.text: When should be a single action

questiontext.text: Which line is the best single When step for a scenario about placing an order?

answer.text: When the customer places the order

feedback.text: Correct — one clear action that triggers the behaviour under test.

answer.text: When the customer adds an item, applies a coupon, and places the order

feedback.text: That bundles several actions; a When should ideally be one event, with setup moved to Given.

answer.text: When the customer is logged in

feedback.text: Being logged in is a precondition (Given), not the action under test.

answer.text: When the order confirmation is displayed

feedback.text: That is an observable outcome (Then), not the action.

generalfeedback.text: A well-formed scenario has one When: the single action whose result you verify. Preceding setup (adding items, applying coupons) belongs in Given steps; the confirmation shown afterwards belongs in Then.

name.text: Then is an outcome, not an action

questiontext.text: Which line is an appropriate Then step (an observable outcome)?

answer.text: Then the account balance is 70

feedback.text: Correct — an observable result that the scenario can verify.

answer.text: Then the user clicks "Confirm"

feedback.text: Clicking is an action (When); a Then should observe a result, not perform an action.

answer.text: Then the user is logged in with a valid session

feedback.text: That reads as a precondition (Given) or setup, not the outcome being verified here.

answer.text: Then enter the withdrawal amount

feedback.text: Entering an amount is an action (When), not an observable outcome.

generalfeedback.text: Then states something observable that should hold after the action, such as a resulting balance, a message, or a visible state. Putting an action (a click, an input) into a Then confuses the outcome with the event and is a common anti-pattern.

name.text: What a step definition does at run time

questiontext.text: When a BDD tool runs the step When the user withdraws 30, what happens?

answer.text: The tool finds the step definition whose pattern matches that text and executes its code against the system

feedback.text: Correct — the step text is matched to glue code, which is then run.

answer.text: The tool prints the line and moves on without executing anything

feedback.text: Steps are executed via their step definitions, not merely printed.

answer.text: The tool rewrites the Gherkin into production source code

feedback.text: BDD tools run scenarios via step definitions; they do not generate production code.

answer.text: The tool asks the user to confirm the outcome manually

feedback.text: Execution is automated through step definitions, not confirmed by hand.

generalfeedback.text: Each Gherkin step is matched at run time to a step definition — glue code whose pattern captures the step's text (and any parameters). The tool executes that code to drive the application, then reports the step (and scenario) as pass or fail.

name.text: And inherits the previous keyword's type

questiontext.text:
In this scenario, what type of step is the And line?

Given the user is logged in
And the user is an administrator
When the user opens the settings page
Then the audit log is shown

answer.text: A Given (precondition) — And inherits the type of the step above it

feedback.text: Correct — And after a Given is itself a Given.

answer.text: A When (action) — And always means an action

feedback.text: And has no fixed type; here it follows a Given, so it is a precondition.

answer.text: A Then (outcome) — And always checks a result

feedback.text: And inherits the prior keyword; following a Given it is a precondition, not an outcome.

answer.text: It is ignored because And is not a real keyword

feedback.text: And is a real continuation keyword; the step runs and here counts as a Given.

generalfeedback.text: And (and But) continue whatever phase preceded them. Because the line above is a Given, "And the user is an administrator" is a second precondition — another Given.

questiontext.text: An Examples table for a Scenario Outline has a header row followed by 4 data rows. How many concrete scenarios run?

answer.text: 4 — one per data row

feedback.text: Correct — the header is not a run; the 4 data rows give 4 scenarios.

answer.text: 5 — the header row counts too

feedback.text: The header only labels columns; only the 4 data rows run.

answer.text: 1 — outlines run once

feedback.text: An outline runs once per data row, so 4 rows give 4 runs.

answer.text: 8 — data rows are doubled

feedback.text: Each data row runs exactly once, giving 4, not 8.

generalfeedback.text: The number of runs equals the number of data rows in the Examples table. A header row plus 4 data rows means 4 executions of the outline.

questiontext.text: Every scenario in a feature needs a logged-in user before doing anything else. Which step is the right one to place in Background?

answer.text: Given the user is logged in

feedback.text: Correct — a common precondition shared by all scenarios belongs in Background.

answer.text: When the user deletes their account

feedback.text: A scenario-specific action does not belong in shared Background setup.

answer.text: Then the dashboard is displayed

feedback.text: Outcomes are per-scenario Then steps, not shared Background setup.

answer.text: Examples: | plan | price |

feedback.text: An Examples table drives a Scenario Outline; it is not Background setup.

generalfeedback.text: Background holds the setup common to every scenario in the feature, which is almost always Given preconditions such as "Given the user is logged in". Actions and outcomes stay inside individual scenarios.

questiontext.text: In a Scenario Outline, what does a step placeholder like <price> refer to?

answer.text: The value in the column headed "price" of the current Examples row, substituted for each run

feedback.text: Correct — placeholders are filled from the matching Examples column per row.

answer.text: A random value the tool generates for each run

feedback.text: Placeholders take fixed values from the Examples table, not random ones.

answer.text: The name of a step definition to call

feedback.text: Placeholders are data slots; step definitions are matched by the step text.

answer.text: A comment that the tool ignores

feedback.text: Placeholders are substituted with real data; they are not comments.

generalfeedback.text: Each <placeholder> in a Scenario Outline is replaced, for every run, by the value under the matching column header in the current Examples row. This is how one outline covers many data cases concisely.

questiontext.text: What is the main purpose of tags (e.g. @smoke) on Gherkin scenarios?

answer.text: To label scenarios so runs can be filtered, grouped, or given hooks (e.g. run only @smoke scenarios)

feedback.text: Correct — tags categorise scenarios for selective execution and hooks.

answer.text: To assert the expected outcome of a scenario

feedback.text: Outcomes are Then steps; tags are labels for organising and filtering runs.

answer.text: To supply data rows to a Scenario Outline

feedback.text: Data rows come from Examples; tags are metadata labels.

answer.text: To define the glue code for a step

feedback.text: Glue code is in step definitions; tags simply categorise scenarios.

generalfeedback.text: Tags are metadata annotations on features or scenarios. They let you select subsets to run (e.g. only @smoke or @wip), organise reports, and attach setup/teardown hooks to tagged scenarios.

questiontext.text: What is the conventional order of the three main step phases within a scenario?

answer.text: Given (context), then When (action), then Then (outcome)

feedback.text: Correct — context first, then the action, then the outcome to verify.

answer.text: Then, then When, then Given

feedback.text: That reverses the flow; context must be established before the action and outcome.

answer.text: When, then Given, then Then

feedback.text: The precondition (Given) comes before the action (When), not after.

answer.text: The order does not matter at all

feedback.text: The Given/When/Then order reflects context to action to outcome and should be followed.

generalfeedback.text: A scenario reads as a small story: Given sets the context, When performs the action, and Then verifies the observable outcome. This context to action to outcome order is what makes scenarios readable.

questiontext.text:
Which keyword completes the middle line, which is the event that triggers the behaviour?

Given the article is in the "draft" state
___ the author publishes the article
Then the article is visible to readers

answer.text: When

feedback.text: Correct — publishing the article is the triggering action, so it is a When.

answer.text: Given

feedback.text: The precondition (draft state) is already the Given; the action is a When.

answer.text: Then

feedback.text: Then is the visible-to-readers outcome; the publishing action is a When.

answer.text: Examples

feedback.text: Examples supply data rows to an outline; the action line is a When.

generalfeedback.text: The scenario starts in a draft state (Given), the author performs the publish action (When), and the article becoming visible is the verified outcome (Then). The middle line is the action, so it takes When.

name.text: Critique: multiple behaviours in one scenario

questiontext.text:
What is the main problem with this scenario?

Scenario: account operations
  Given the balance is 100
  When the user deposits 50
  Then the balance is 150
  When the user withdraws 30
  Then the balance is 120

answer.text: It tests two distinct behaviours (deposit and withdrawal) in one scenario; each behaviour should be its own scenario with a single When/Then focus

feedback.text: Correct — one behaviour per scenario keeps failures diagnosable and scenarios readable.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; multiple When/Then pairs are the recommended style

feedback.text: Chaining multiple When/Then pairs mixes behaviours; split them into separate scenarios.

answer.text: The Given must come after the first Then

feedback.text: Given correctly comes first; the real issue is two behaviours in one scenario.

answer.text: Balances are not allowed in Gherkin steps

feedback.text: Concrete values are fine; the problem is combining two behaviours in one scenario.

generalfeedback.text: A scenario should illustrate one behaviour with essentially one When and its Then. Chaining When/Then/When/Then bundles deposit and withdrawal together, so a failure is harder to localise and the scenario is harder to read. Split it into two focused scenarios.

name.text: Fix a scenario with multiple When steps

questiontext.text:
A scenario reads:

Given I am on the checkout page
When I enter my address
When I enter my card details
When I click "Pay"
Then the order is confirmed

What is the best improvement?

answer.text: Treat entering address and card details as setup (Given/And) and keep a single When for the "Pay" action that triggers the behaviour

feedback.text: Correct — reserve When for the one triggering action and move the rest to setup.

answer.text: Merge all three actions into one long When sentence joined by "and"

feedback.text: That just hides several actions in one step; better to make the earlier ones setup and keep one triggering When.

answer.text: Convert every When into a Then

feedback.text: Then is for outcomes; the actions are not outcomes, so this is wrong.

answer.text: Delete the Then so only actions remain

feedback.text: Removing the outcome leaves nothing to verify; the fix is to have one clear When.

generalfeedback.text: The behaviour under test is "paying" confirms the order. Entering address and card details are preconditions, so they read better as Given/And setup, leaving a single When ("I click Pay") whose Then checks the confirmation. One action per When keeps the scenario focused.

questiontext.text: Why are declarative, business-level scenarios generally preferred over imperative UI-step scenarios?

answer.text: They express intent independent of UI mechanics, so they read clearly to business stakeholders and do not break when buttons, ids, or layouts change

feedback.text: Correct — declarative scenarios are more readable and far less brittle.

answer.text: They run faster because they skip the step definitions

feedback.text: Both styles run through step definitions; the benefit is readability and robustness, not speed.

answer.text: They make the Examples table unnecessary in every case

feedback.text: Examples relate to data-driven outlines; that is unrelated to declarative style.

answer.text: They allow multiple When steps without any downside

feedback.text: Declarative style is about intent versus UI detail, not about permitting many Whens.

generalfeedback.text: Declarative scenarios describe what the user wants to accomplish, pushing UI mechanics (clicks, selectors, field ids) down into step definitions. This keeps scenarios readable as shared documentation and stable across UI redesigns, whereas imperative scenarios break whenever the interface changes.

questiontext.text:
What is wrong with this step?

Given the account balance should be 100

answer.text: It phrases a Given as an assertion ("should be"); Given must set up state ("the balance is 100"), while assertions belong in Then

feedback.text: Correct — a Given establishes context, it does not verify anything.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; Given steps normally contain assertions

feedback.text: Given is setup, not verification; assertions belong in Then.

answer.text: Given may not mention numbers

feedback.text: Numbers are fine; the issue is that a precondition should not be an assertion.

answer.text: The step should start with When instead

feedback.text: It is a precondition, so Given is the right phase; it just must state, not assert.

generalfeedback.text: Given establishes a known state of the world; it should read as a fact being set up ("the balance is 100"), not as something to be checked ("should be"). Turning setup into an assertion muddles precondition and outcome — assertions belong in Then.

name.text: Misuse: a UI click inside Then

questiontext.text:
What is the problem with this final step?

Given I am viewing my cart
When I proceed to checkout
Then I click "Place order"

answer.text: Then contains an action (a click), but Then must state an observable outcome; the click is an action that belongs in a When

feedback.text: Correct — Then verifies a result; it should not perform an action.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; Then steps commonly perform clicks

feedback.text: Then should observe, not act; a click belongs in When.

answer.text: The scenario has too few steps to be valid

feedback.text: Step count is not the issue; the Then step wrongly performs an action.

answer.text: Then must always come before When

feedback.text: Then comes after When; the real problem is that the Then performs an action.

generalfeedback.text: Then asserts an observable outcome after the action. Putting a click ("Place order") in a Then confuses the outcome with a new action; that click is itself an event and belongs in a When, with the resulting confirmation checked in Then.

name.text: And after When is an action step

questiontext.text:
In this scenario, what phase does the And line belong to?

Given I am logged in
When I enter a search term
And I press "Search"
Then results are displayed

answer.text: A When (action) — And inherits the type of the When above it

feedback.text: Correct — following a When, the And is another action step.

answer.text: A Given (precondition) — And is always setup

feedback.text: And has no fixed type; here it follows a When, so it is an action.

answer.text: A Then (outcome) — And is always an assertion

feedback.text: And inherits the prior keyword; after a When it is an action, not an outcome.

answer.text: It has no type and is skipped

feedback.text: And executes as a real step and here counts as part of the When phase.

generalfeedback.text: And continues the phase of the most recent Given/When/Then above it. Because it follows a When, "And I press Search" is an action step. (Note that two Whens like this often signal that some of the actions should really be setup.)

questiontext.text: Why does BDD stress using a ubiquitous (shared) language in scenarios?

answer.text: So business, developers, and testers describe behaviour with the same domain terms, reducing miscommunication and keeping the specification meaningful to everyone

feedback.text: Correct — a shared vocabulary aligns the whole team on what the behaviour means.

answer.text: So scenarios can be written only by programmers

feedback.text: The opposite — shared language lets non-programmers read and contribute too.

answer.text: So the tool can generate production code automatically

feedback.text: Shared language is about communication, not code generation.

answer.text: So scenarios run faster at test time

feedback.text: Shared language improves understanding, not execution speed.

generalfeedback.text: A ubiquitous language uses consistent domain terms across conversation, scenarios, and code. It closes the gap between what the business means and what developers build, so the executable specification stays a trustworthy shared description of behaviour.

questiontext.text: In what sense are BDD scenarios living documentation?

answer.text: Because they are executed against the system, a passing suite means the documentation still matches actual behaviour, so it cannot silently go stale

feedback.text: Correct — executable scenarios stay in sync with the system as it changes.

answer.text: Because they are printed on paper and archived

feedback.text: Living documentation is executable and kept current, not a static archive.

answer.text: Because a technical writer rewrites them after every release

feedback.text: The point is that execution keeps them current automatically, not manual rewriting.

answer.text: Because they can only be read, never run

feedback.text: They are run against the system; that is exactly what keeps them alive.

generalfeedback.text: Traditional documents drift from the code over time. BDD scenarios are executed, so if behaviour changes without updating the scenarios, they fail. A green suite is evidence the documentation still describes the real system — documentation that stays alive.

questiontext.text: Which scenario title/step combination most clearly violates the "one behaviour per scenario" guideline?

answer.text: A scenario titled "user management" that in one body registers a user, then logs them in, then deletes the account, each with its own Then

feedback.text: Correct — that bundles three separate behaviours into one scenario.

answer.text: A scenario "successful login" with one When (log in) and one Then (dashboard shown)

feedback.text: That is a single, well-focused behaviour — not a violation.

answer.text: A scenario "withdraw within balance" with a Given, a single When, and a single Then

feedback.text: That is one behaviour with a clear action and outcome — not a violation.

answer.text: A scenario "empty cart shows message" with a Given and a single Then

feedback.text: That checks one behaviour; it is not a violation.

generalfeedback.text: A scenario that registers, logs in, and deletes an account tests three behaviours at once. Each should be its own scenario so failures are localised and each reads as one clear example. Focused single-behaviour scenarios are the correct pattern.

questiontext.text:
Why is this Background block a poor design?

Background:
  Given the user is logged in
  When the user deletes their most recent order

answer.text: Background should contain shared setup (Givens), not an action; the When forces a behaviour-changing action before every scenario, which distorts the tests

feedback.text: Correct — Background is for common context, not for performing actions.

answer.text: Background may not contain any steps at all

feedback.text: Background does contain steps — it is just meant for shared setup, not actions.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; running an action before each scenario is recommended

feedback.text: Running a behaviour-changing action before every scenario is exactly the anti-pattern here.

answer.text: Background must appear after the scenarios, not before

feedback.text: Background is placed before scenarios; the real issue is the action step in it.

generalfeedback.text: Background factors out common context and should hold Given setup only. Putting a When (a state-changing action) there runs that action before every scenario, mixing setup with behaviour and making scenarios depend on a side effect. Keep actions inside the scenarios that test them.

name.text: Misuse: a Given that performs an action

questiontext.text:
A scenario about withdrawal begins:

Given the user withdraws 30 from the account
When the balance is checked
Then it shows 70

What is the flaw?

answer.text: The withdrawal — the actual behaviour under test — is buried in a Given as if it were setup; the withdrawal should be the When, with a Given establishing the starting balance

feedback.text: Correct — the action to be tested must be the When, not hidden in a Given.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; the action is fine as a Given

feedback.text: The action under test should be the When; placing it in Given misframes the scenario.

answer.text: The Then must state an action, not a number

feedback.text: Then correctly states an outcome; the flaw is the action placed in the Given.

answer.text: Scenarios may not check a balance

feedback.text: Checking a balance is fine; the problem is the misplaced action in the Given.

generalfeedback.text: The behaviour being tested is the withdrawal, so it should be the When. A better form is: "Given the balance is 100 / When the user withdraws 30 / Then the balance is 70." Hiding the action in a Given treats the very thing under test as mere setup.

name.text: Scenario Outline expansion with two Examples tables

questiontext.text:
How many concrete scenarios does this Scenario Outline produce?

Scenario Outline: discount by tier
  When a <tier> customer checks out
  Then the discount is <pct>%

  Examples: standard tiers
    | tier   | pct |
    | bronze | 0   |
    | silver | 5   |

  Examples: premium tiers
    | tier     | pct |
    | gold     | 10  |
    | platinum | 15  |
    | diamond  | 20  |

answer.text: 5 — 2 data rows from the first table plus 3 from the second

feedback.text: Correct — runs equal the total data rows across all Examples tables: 2 + 3 = 5.

answer.text: 2 — only the first Examples table counts

feedback.text: Both Examples tables contribute; the total is 2 + 3 = 5.

answer.text: 6 — 2 multiplied by 3

feedback.text: Tables add their rows, they are not multiplied: 2 + 3 = 5.

answer.text: 7 — the two header rows count as runs too

feedback.text: Header rows never count; only the 5 data rows run.

generalfeedback.text: A Scenario Outline may have more than one Examples table; it runs once per data row across all of them. Here 2 data rows plus 3 data rows give 5 concrete scenarios (header rows are not counted).

name.text: Spec by example and executable specification

questiontext.text: What is meant by "specification by example" / an executable specification in BDD?

answer.text: Concrete examples of desired behaviour are written so precisely that they can be executed directly as automated acceptance tests, serving as both specification and verification

feedback.text: Correct — the examples are the spec and can be run to verify the system.

answer.text: A separate specification document is written first and the examples are discarded before coding

feedback.text: The examples are not discarded; they become the executable spec itself.

answer.text: Examples are only used to illustrate a spec but can never be run

feedback.text: The point is precisely that they can be run — that is what makes them executable.

answer.text: It means writing production code first and adding examples afterwards

feedback.text: BDD drives from examples outward; the examples specify behaviour before/with implementation.

generalfeedback.text: Specification by example captures requirements as concrete, agreed examples. Written in Gherkin and backed by step definitions, those examples run as acceptance tests: they specify what the system should do and simultaneously verify that it does, collapsing spec and test into one artefact.

questiontext.text: How does BDD relate to TDD and ATDD?

answer.text: BDD evolved from TDD, shifting emphasis to behaviour described in shared language; like ATDD it drives development from acceptance-level examples agreed with the business (outside-in)

feedback.text: Correct — BDD is a behaviour- and collaboration-focused evolution of TDD, closely aligned with ATDD.

answer.text: BDD replaces all testing and makes unit tests unnecessary

feedback.text: BDD complements, not replaces, unit-level TDD; both have their place.

answer.text: BDD is unrelated to TDD and forbids writing tests before code

feedback.text: BDD grew out of TDD and still favours specifying behaviour before/with implementation.

answer.text: BDD is only about performance testing

feedback.text: BDD is about specifying functional behaviour by example, not performance testing.

generalfeedback.text: TDD drives code from failing unit tests. BDD reframes this around behaviour expressed in ubiquitous language and readable examples, working outside-in from acceptance criteria — much like ATDD (acceptance-test-driven development). The three share the "tests/examples first" spirit at different levels of granularity.

name.text: A single Examples data row runs once

questiontext.text: A Scenario Outline whose Examples table has a header row and exactly one data row will run exactly one concrete scenario.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — one data row means one run; the header row is not counted.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: It does run once: the number of runs equals the number of data rows, which is one here.

generalfeedback.text: The number of concrete scenarios a Scenario Outline produces equals the number of data rows in its Examples table(s). With a single data row (plus the header, which never counts), it runs exactly once — behaving like an ordinary scenario with those values substituted.
